blocks.x: I played piano with Ruth Lowe the other day. You know the joke, can you play piano? I don't know, I never tried. I was sitting down there, I know three chords on the piano, and Ruth Lowe and Morgan were there, and there was a photographer there, so I started playing away on the piano. And I played the, you know, in C, I played C, G, and F, you know, C, F, and G, you know, in the right order sometimes, and sometimes in time, it was fun.
It doesn't fix me, you know. I think...
Let me know if I'm over-modulating, man.
I think you're good, Shane.
Okay, what do you want to ask, Beth?
Well...
She's got to get to that.
Mostly just, I guess, about your association with Louis Armstrong,
since you're both sick right now.

Well, about me and Louis, I'll tell you about that. Uh... I left the country in 1918, and I was 18 years old. I went to World War I, and when I came back, the first people I saw was playing at the 25, Louis Armstrong, Kid Ory, Johnny Dots, Baby Dots, and Bob Lyons on bass, and Lorenzo Starrs on guitar, so... You had to play in a drum?
Who was it? Baby Dots.
Baby Dots.
Baby Dots, isn't it? Yeah, go ahead.

Oh, sure. Baby Dots. And, uh... So somebody made me acquainted with Ori. I don't know who it was, but... And he asked me to come up and blow some. This is... This is no joke. This is real. So I went up and blowed. I blowed me some army numbers. I blowed me some blues, and I blowed me some songs, you know. So they said, oh, yeah. And Lorenzo said, look out there. He said, you better watch out, say, there's somebody gonna get you. And Lorenzo said to him, well, let him get me. That's all right. I quit. I quit. And Lorenzo's gotta quit. But that's true. Yeah, he literally got mad, you know. But he... They were just joking, you know.
Yeah. When did you learn Smiles Bunch?
In the Army.
In the Army.
Oh, that was my crips, Smiles. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Did you always continue playing that number?
I play that number right now at times.
Yeah? Did you play the 25 of them?
Yeah. I know it. I brought it in there. He didn't know that.
No? No, he didn't know that.
You brought it in there with what band? Just me.
Just me.
I sat in the band. Sitting in what band?
In Kid Ora's band. Oh, in Kid Ora's band.
Yeah. Could Louie cut it?
No, he didn't know it then. He didn't know it. But he played the author.
Yeah. I guess you're scared of it, huh? Well, you just went in there. Did you borrow an instrument that time?
No, I had my instrument in my hand. I stole it out there on me. Put it in my bag. And I looked down there and put it in my bag.
Did you always carry it with you? When you went to the different-

Well, I played it long until they filled out the keys one day, one night at least. Straight on the upper line of the street, I think it was. And the keys didn't lock good, and I forgot about it. They dropped in a barrel, and they weren't there with no more good. So I carried it to the phone shelf, and I jived them by the way I just played on the two valves, and they're talking, give me fifteen dollars. So that's what I just got to come with that one. But I got another one right away, huh?
Did you sleep with your trumpet? Yeah.
You wouldn't let it out of your-
Except that trumpet. You didn't really sleep with your trumpet, did you? In the bed?
Yeah. I had to. I had no case with the second one I got. Yeah, the second one.
And you didn't have any case? And you actually would put it in bed with?
Put it right down in the pillow, man. I was kidding.
Where were you staying?
Where were you staying then? In a boarding house?

No, I was living in a place called Jack Kerry. He had a wooden coal place, and I was playing, I joined his bands, and he gave me a place to stay there. But it was pretty sad, though. Yeah. Oh, no, it was sad. It was sad.
How much did Jack call you, charge you to stay there?
He didn't charge me nothing. I was playing the band with him, and he just gave me the place to sleep.
And you slept on the coal side? Yeah. No, did you? What did you sleep on? The day count.
The day count, yeah. He shut it up in the day and opened it up at night, you know. Oh, yeah.
What about, who did Doc Ernest have on trumpet then?
Well, I was just a fights band I played with.
Yeah.

But I didn't stay with him for maybe a week, because Jack Kerry would come out there, and everybody was talking about Jack Kerry, you know. So I said, I believe I joined Jack Kerry. And I joined Jack Kerry. And I joined Jack Kerry. And I went on up. He had a big name. He had a big name. And after that, the boy, let me tell you this, you see. You see, everybody, leader of a band was a trumpet player. Keith Rennie, Buddy Patee, Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly, all of them were trumpet players. That's all your bunch? Now wait, now no. In a different band. So everybody, people didn't know me, they thought I was Jack Kerry. See, everybody around there called me Jack Kerry, but I wasn't Jack Kerry. Jack Kerry was the trombone player. See, he did the trombone player. See, he did the trombone player. So the boy said, look, Princey, you getting all that felicity for somebody else, you ought to let it go out in your name for real. So they all quit Jack and we made up a band. And I ran on the plan. And I just, and I ran on top. I mean, I did good. I did good. I did good. I did good all the way. What did you call it?
Punching his bunch.
In them kinds. What about the Zulus? Did you play for them much? Oh, I played for the Zulus about seven or eight different years.
Really? Yeah. Man, I could walk then. I didn't play parades.
Just about, I'd say about seven years I quit walking. What was it with the Zulus? What kind of parade would they have? Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Zulus parade, they call it. Come on.
All right. How you doing? Go ahead, finish your conversation, babe. Zulus parade. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. No. Hold it a minute, can you? Sure, we can hold it.
No, I say, now we'll interview you. Huh? Now we'll interview you. That was W. J. Oliver. He was probably a relative of King Oliver's from up around Donaldsonville. He works here in the hospital.
He was a little brass band and different guys in the town of the
Oh, that's Aureus drummer, Henry Martin. That's the same guy?
He was a snare drummer.
Yeah.
He played trumpet drums too, but he had to play snare drums in the parade. Yeah. And the big old Carnie. Mm-hmm.
You heard it? Willie Cornish, yeah.
Yeah. And, uh, I can't think of it. But anyhow, Franky Dusen on trombone.
You must have had a tuba player.
Yeah, but I'm going to tell you. Franky Dusen on trombone. And I can't call this name, but he used to hang at Ramport and Petita all the time. Not Bob Lyon. Bob Lyon played bass violin.
What did this man play?
He played tuba, bass tuba.
Big star-frog. Was he a friend of Dandy Lewis and those guys? No, that's right.
Uh, Willie, I called his name. He used to play. Willie Cornish? That's who played tuba. Willie Cornish played tuba?
I know his name Willie. Yeah, Willie, yeah.
Big Cornish.
Big Cornish, yeah. Yeah, that's Willie Cornish. Married that young girl. Yeah, that's the man. I knew her. You remember? Yeah.
Yeah.
Boy, that was funny. That was the funniest of the way.
Yeah. Yeah. Boy, that was funny. That was Louis Armstrong that played with you in the Zulu.
Did Louis play with you ever?
In the band?
In the brass band.
Oh, I see.
In the Zulu parade? Uh-huh.
Zulus?
Yeah, well, he and Black Benny were real good buddies. Black Benny looked after Louis, you see, when he was a kid. You can read that up in the book. No, I didn't.

Black Benny was crazy about me and Louis. Mm-hmm. And, uh, so that's probably the best I can tell you now about brass band. I can't remember it all. Oh, no. But Louis would go to 25 at night, and I would go to Astorias. Oh, yeah. See? He'd have to pass my place every night. He'd stop and stand up. I'd be upstairs. Mm-hmm. Wave, wave, wave, wave, and whatnot. And the next big parade, we'd get together on that.
Mm-hmm.
Was Louis married then? No.
Uh-uh. Not then.
Um, have you talked to him? What's, when is the last time you talked to him?
Louis? Uh, I'll be there last viester.
Last festival?
Last year.
Last year.
But I get mail from him all the time.
Oh, he writes you letters, huh? Yeah, yeah, yeah. I'd like to see some of those letters.
Yeah, well, I got them at the house.

Well, I may be in touch with Lucille. Yeah. So I'll try to tell her you know that you're doing better. Yeah. You're feeling better? Mm-hmm. And they got you laying. He's in the hospital, too. Yeah. You're laying in the bed like an alligator, huh? No. Not so. Hey, you too bad to interview yesterday, huh, man? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, he didn't feel like it yesterday. Uh, well, I came to make him feel better. Yeah, sure. Yeah, he feels great. Yeah, now he feels good. Yeah, I'm doing all right today. Yeah.
What did, um, did you have any nicknames besides Kid and Punch ever?
Well, the only nickname I have was Punch. But now my sisters, they had two sisters, one died. Yeah, yeah.
And my middle of the old step there.
They all called me Bud. They all called you Bud?
Bud. But the people outside called me Punch.
And what did you call them? Because I was a twin, see, they called us Punch and Judah.
Uh-huh. What did your niece call you? Uncle Bud? Or a little Lionel used to call you Uncle Bud. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
I heard Uncle Bud. Well, she called me Uncle Bud. No. Sometimes, sometimes she called me Uncle Lionel.
But you're not the same Uncle Bud they sing songs about?
No.
Oh, thank you. I'll tell you about that laugh there.
Well, how about that? We can get on to it, but you got all that stuff.
Yeah, but we don't know about you and Louis. That's the thing she wants to know.
Well, I'm not.
She might put your picture in a magazine. You'll be rich and famous. Yeah, well, no.
More than we used to play in the same brass band.
You didn't know him in Chicago or technical?

No, no. Oh, yeah. I thought, he lived in 26, I think. And I left here in 1927. Uh-huh. Well, we'd meet on the street like that and talk. And sometime he'd tell me he had a few jobs or something like that. He'd put me with a band. I played every Sunday with that band. There's two brothers of them. I can't call their name. Was that near the Vendal?
That's what I told you about. Near the Vendal.

Oh, yeah. Well, I got up, started to make a solo. Yeah. And there had a light. Let's light that light there. I didn't know nothing about the light, see. And I jumped up, took a solo, and that light went on to me. Yeah. I'd see me fogging going on. I never did that. But I did all right there. I did all good. And I never get a jam session. Some guy was standing outside, so I was playing at a place called The Bookstove. We had about four pieces. So Joe, Joe, Joe Smith and Russell Smith, two brothers. Yeah. Joe said, go get him. Russell and Russell said, no, I ain't gonna bother him. Louis said, you go get him, Joe. Joe said, I'm going to get him. And he went in. I blow so much horn, man. He packed up right in front of everybody in the place. Just pack his horn up left. Well, he was a beautiful-
I had to play. I had to play then.
He couldn't do with me.
He was a beautiful blues man, but I don't think he could have cut you all around then.
Well, him and his brother played with flutcher, you know.
Yeah, but his brother was more of a straight man.
Oh, his brother was a straight trumpet player, Russell.
Could he get off at all?
No. He was a straight horn.
What was one of the greatest audiences you ever played for, one of the greatest times?
What'd you say? What's the best audience you ever played for, the greatest time you ever had, you know, playing for people?

Well, I'm gonna tell you the truth. The biggest time I ever had, the biggest money I ever made, it happened funny. I was living in Chicago then. So, a guy come to me to make up a band to take a excursion from Chicago to Memphis, Tennessee. Well, when we get in Memphis, he asked everybody, he asked them, see, how much y'all want? Y'all want to play on percentage, or y'all want to just pay? No, no, we don't play on percentage. See, this pay us off twelve dollars a man a night, for the night. So, he said, okay. He said, Punch, you want to play on percentage? I said, yeah, man, percentage. And that big yard, great big yard, Dick. And that great big place where the dance at. And that yard was full, the pack, all was packing jam and everything. So, he paid them the twelve dollars a man, and he gave me five hundred dollars. Five hundred dollars. And then they made money. That fella looked like me. He was charging a dollar and a half at the gate. At the gate. When was that?
Oh, that guy.
Wow.
What band were you with?
A band I made up from Chicago, my band.
From Chicago. Yeah. We just made them up. We got together and made them. After the Depression hit or before the Depression hit? No.
No, it was before the Depression. Yeah.
Before Bill came back or after Bill came back? No. Oh, you got me down. Yeah.
Okay. Would you know that there, Mr. Waldey? Who? Mr. Waldey.
I don't know. Not August Waldey.
Oh, this is my son. No.
Yeah. Oh.
They said, well, 11, this is 11. 5-11?
Henry, maybe. Maybe. I heard of Henry, but I don't know.
Okay.
I don't know. I happen to know the family, but I don't know that one. Yeah. I'm back and I'm back. Yeah. And this one right now. Yeah.
What you in? What you in?
was the... Depression hit in 1929, the end of 1929. I was in Chicago. You were in Chicago. But this excursion was before then. Before then, so it was about 28 or 27. He arrived in Chicago in
27, so we got it pretty well pinpointed to one or three years. Yeah, 28 I think.
About around that time, and the fella kind of looked like me, that had the joint, had the yard,
and you told me about him once. Yeah, yeah. Comes back to me. That's the most money I've made in one night in my life.
Did anyone ever not pay you that was supposed to pay you? Well, yeah. We went to a girl pool,
it was a girl from the Boogalooza, Louisiana, and a guy made a lot of money there that night, and he tipped away, stole away. We caught the train and went to California. We ain't seen him since.
Yeah. You know, a friend of mine said he used to give you the mule all the time. You know what that is?

Yeah, I know, but they ain't give me no mule all the time. No, I got my money. That's the only time I ever, I ever, you know, got slipped with my money. Well, this guy's rich. He has a, I'm getting that thing. He has a hardware store. He had a good load of money, I know, because he's charging, I think about 75 cents at the door. This is the guy from Boogalooza to California? Yeah, but he, but that was a great big, uh, pavilion, you know, pavilion. And, uh, so he come up to us by just about the middle of the night and say, how y'all doing? I say, all right, got a drink for us. And next time we looked, that guy was gone. Cut the deep train, got away from me. Uh-huh. But we had money, everyone has had money.
He's been waking up and he's been sleeping since I came in here. It was two and five.
What, what about some of the, uh, young musicians? Have you heard any young musicians or some of the newer, newer kinds of music that you like?

Young ones? Uh-huh. Yeah, well, in Japan, they got young fellas playing the same stuff with me. In Japan, and, uh, you know, London, England. Uh-huh. And with them, but these young boys here, they want to land rock and roll. But them boys land old Dixieland over there, and they does go too. What about rock and roll? What do you think of that?
It's all right, but it's more for young people. Uh-huh. You wouldn't dance to it then?
I couldn't dance, but I tell you, there's a lot of young people come to the Preservation Hall,
and this time. Lots of people. Young people, I mean, young people. They like it. They like rock and roll.
I mean, they're jazz. Why do you think young people like jazz still? Huh? Why do you think young people still like it?
You say, why do they like it? Uh-huh. Well, to my idea, the old people are telling me, so what's about it? And they want to hear, you know what I mean? You hear what it's all about.
What do the young people think? I miss it.

Well, she said, why do the young people like Dixieland? Yeah. I said, because the old people talk to them about it, tell them about it. Oh, I see. And they go out with them, and lots of them just fall for it, go for it.
Uh-huh. Put your friends to the cage.
Like Tommy Sancton. Yeah, yeah.
He's better than ever, they say on clarinet.
Yeah, that boy play more clarinet. He's a young kid, he. Is he 20? He's about 20.
21, 22. I saw his daddy yesterday.
Yeah, you did? He probably, I talked to him on the phone a few nights ago, he probably could come by, but I guess he'd be busy.
He has. He was reading up on Louis.
When you were in the military band, in the army, that was the army, and he was a young man. How many people were in that band? About 65, I think. Did you learn a lot of new songs there?

Oh, that's where I learned my music at in that band. Let me tell you, I played in the big brass band, I played in the dance band, then I was bugle car. I was right on it. Head voice, drink voice, did everything in front.
Mm-hmm. Well, what did you do, play in parades?
Yeah, they had a parade every evening.
Every evening? Every evening, yeah.
I don't think they do that in honor, but they did then. Every evening we had to march about a mile. Yeah, about a mile.
Down the streets of the town, for the townspeople? No, not the town, in the camp. In the camp.
In the army.
All right.
I don't know who I am. Oh, dear.
Um, well, when you went into the army, did they know that you could play music?

No. I'm going to tell you how that happened. I couldn't play nothing but the blues or anything, but I'll tell you what happened. I was like, how you, uh, the, uh, the, uh, carpool, bugle carpool, had four bugles on his side, four hanging on his side. And he's making an arm, and he said, anybody got a professional, or what they want to do, that's the professional, that's the job. So I walked up to him, I walked out of line, out of line, I said, how about blowing one in the bugle? Oh, I'll give you a bell. He said, that's all right, can you blow it? And I put your, that, that, that, that is, oh, yeah, you all right. He said.
What did you play for him? Just, what did you play for him? What did I play? That time, what did you play?

Nothing but a bugle call. Oh, uh-huh. The bugle, that was the bugle, wasn't the trumpet, it was the bugle. So I played the bugle call, and I did all right for the brass band, find out I could play trumpet, and he put me in the brass band. That's where I studied. I got a, got a, got a, two hours in the morning, and two hours in the evening, that's all you did.
You just knew how to play blues, you said, when you went in?
When I first went there, that's all I could play mostly.
What, what, what songs did you know?

Well, you wouldn't know them if I could call them. Yes, she would. She used to work for me. I might go listen to them. Wait, wait, wait, we played, uh, what did we play with back then? I'd have forgotten, I swear.
What did Bach play?
Oh, Bach played moist blues. Oh yeah, Alexander Radcliffe band. And, uh, what's that thing there? Over There. I knew what that kind of piece is, but I'd have forgotten.
What about the all the animal dances, you know, that have all those animal dances. Do you know those songs about animals?
I know the monkey and the bear, do you? Yeah?
And what else? And I know, uh, what does that mean? What about the bear?
Didn't you have a song about the bear?
Yeah, wait, wait, wait, wait.
I'm trying to think, oh yeah.
Yeah, that's good.
Um, everybody doing it? Doing it, doing it. Yeah, that's all mama. And, uh, they're coming to me now. Mama love Pa, Papa love Mama too. And, uh, beautiful dog. And, uh, oh, them the old ones.
Did you ever play as a lizard on the rail? Yeah.
On the rail with his tail coupe?
Yeah, I would. Yeah. What about them, uh, Indian novels? Red Wing, did you ever play Red Wing? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. All right. See you later.
What's she asking?
That, well, I know her, uh, know his uncles. They're musicians. All of them. Henry Alvarez. Yeah.
Raymond Burke used to play with his, uh.
What, Raymond Burke?
I call him up last night.
Oh, yeah? Yeah. Raymond Burke used to play with his uncles.
Yeah.
Anyway, it's a small world. Oh, you gotta let go, Punch. Yeah. Now, now hold it like that. It wasn't turning. How does it go?
Everybody doing it, doing it, doing it. Everybody doing it, doing it, doing it. Don't say the ragtime couple over there. Watch them.
You got the mic too close. Let me hold it for you, Punch. Sing. Oh, Lord, I don't mess that up. No. Okay. Go ahead.

Everybody doing it, doing it, doing it. Everybody doing it, doing it, doing it. See that ragtime couple over there. Watch them throw their shoulders in the air. Snap their fingers, honey. I declare it's a bear, it's a bear, it's a bear, bear. Everybody doing it, doing it, doing it. Everybody doing it, doing it, doing it. Don't that music touches your heart to hear that trombone bursting apart. Come, come, come, come, and let us start, darling. Everybody doing it, yes, they all are doing it. Everybody doing it now.
Yeah, that's good, Punch. Everybody doing it. Yeah.
That's the 1920s.
Way back then, way back then. Yeah.
Oh, and I was looking right ahead of that normal.
Yeah. Well, he was ahead of Satch in his day, you know. Are you older? Hmm? And you were older than Lewis?
I'm older than Lewis, sure. You are? I'm four years older than Lewis. I'm supposed to be. Has anybody heard of how is Satch? He's doing better, Satch.
He's doing better, Satch. All right, more Satch.
All right, you know. I got him.
Well, he was holding his own yesterday. He was holding his own yesterday.

That's right. Did you sing Navajo and My Little Napanee and all those songs? No. His uncles used to sing those, one of them, Uncle August. Yeah. And he was a kick, you know, playing in the backyard. They'd have a ball in the backyard. He's the backyard musician.
Yeah, Uncle August was a kick.
I used to do Mama Left Paw.
I don't know that number.
You know?
No. Hold the mic, I'll sing it. Yeah. Is that all right?
Yeah.
Mama Love Paw, Sing straight out.
Relax.

Everything is damn as sweet as can be. Nothing to worry, nothing to worry for me, for me. There's a good reason, a quite good reason. Mama Love Squeezing and Paw, us too. Nothing can break us, nothing can make us blue. We have the bungalow and how we spoon in the evening under the silver moon. People like us, we never fuss. We always have something better to do, cause Mama Love Paw and Paw, Paw and Paw and Paw love my Mama too. Okay. Yeah.
The old numbers there.
Yeah.
Mama Love Paw, Paw, Paw love Mama.
I wish it were true.
Yeah.
Yeah, sometimes I do. But I don't sing them, no, very seldom. I sing the lady. You sing late now?
Oh, yeah. Oh, popular, huh?
Yeah, he knows all the late numbers. You're going to take up rock and roll next, Mark?

No, I know rock and roll, but I can play rock and roll. See, a trumpet ain't got nothing to do but rock and roll with whole notes. The guitar and the drum and bass, violin. They make all this stuff. You just ta, ta, ta, ta, that's all you got to do on drum.
You play lead rhythm on drum. Sure, that's good.
So, you're older than Lewis. That's right. But since you were in the Army, you got started in music.
You see, when I come from the Army, Lewis was in New Orleans at a place called the 25, playing there.
That's when I met him. Huh? Had you heard of him when you met him? Oh, yeah.
I knowed him before I left New Orleans. Was he a big star? No, he wanted nothing then. Oh, no.
How did you know him then?
Well, we all was in homes a while.
You were where?
He caught me on the street, but I wasn't in there but two weeks.
Oh, and the Waves' home together?
Homes, yeah. Old Man Jones' home. Oh, and Jones' home and the Waves' home together?
You were there. You knew him then?
Sure, that's where I first met him. But he couldn't play on the horn. He was just a bad boy, you know.
Well, who else was a bad boy in the home?

Kid Rene. Kid Rene was there then? Sure. Kid Rene. Was that before? I left him. I didn't stay there. But I wanted to stay because they would learn music, see. And I wanted to stay, but they wouldn't let me stay because I come to the country, see.
What about Joe Rene? Was he in the home or out?
Well, yeah, he was in that world, too.
Yeah, but not with you, huh? No, no. And he was in the brass band, too, though, wasn't he? Yeah, that's right, the Zulus. We got an interview with him, too. Excuse me.
Could you play... You were supposed to have taken a... What? Music at 14. So you... When you were in the home, did you play...
Well, yeah, well, I played the blues and things. Nothing but the blues at 14. I know nothing but blues. But the people like it. They play dances. Play different kind of blues. They like it.
Do you miss singing now here in the hospital? Here in the hospital, do you miss singing? Do you...
Do I miss it?
Do you think of writing songs? Or is there something when you're lying in bed?
Well, no, I haven't sung it this time. I just think I'm getting out of here.
Why don't you write a song called Cock Robin? That'll make a good song, wouldn't it, Paul? Oh, yeah. He has. I like that number. Yeah.
How do the words to that work?
You don't have to sing it. But what is it about being in the... Well, I have to sing... In the winter, in the cold?
I have to sing it to get straight.
Oh, well, don't sing it. Don't strain your voice.
I strain it.
Yeah.

One day the sun was warm and bright, no clouds seen in the sky. Miss Robin said to the little one, it's time you all should fly. And every little Robin said to Mom, I'll try, I'll try, I'll try. Sure I know the child and the good one, so I'll try.

Tell you all by and by. But you got to fly, fly, fly, fly. Every little one got to fly high. Fly, fly, fly high. Before mother die. It was well as winter when time was rough. I was in the weather strutting my stuff. So fly, fly, fly, fly. Every little one got to fly high.

I knew she'd get a kick out of that. You remember when that girl came around to see you? Her name was Irish Turner Kelso in the hospital. We got a nice interview and you sang that song. She's from Mississippi. Her cousin was editor of the New York Times. That's what I'm trying to say. You see her on the TV now. Them guys late too. That's her. She's the one who called you.
No, I ain't talking about them three guys. Three guys? Yeah. They must be at three o'clock. But I mean, they'll be all right.
Yeah, well, don't worry about it.
I'm not worried about it.
We'll leave when they come. Your ring, did someone give this to you for good luck?
No, I bought that ring. You know why you bought it? Hmm?
No.
Tell them why you bought it, Ponce.
I bought it for good luck. I bought it at a... Well, don't drop it.
That's bad luck.
What do you name? Oh. Johnny Reef or something on it. What do you name?
On Rampaw at the Hawk Show?
No. No, I know our boy. That's Jack Rose.

Oh, yeah. I know. About stuff. Hmm. What were we talking about, the bulls? Oh, didn't he ramble, huh? You know the words that the bulls used to say? Bulls? Yeah, didn't they have words to that? Zutty told me about that one. Oh, you pleaded?
I just pleaded.
You played for me. Did you play with Denny Ramble?
Oh, yeah.
They liked that.

segments.title: Opening chatter and setting up the Louis Armstrong interview
segments.summary: Interviewers joke about playing piano, check recording levels, and say the interview is mainly about Punch's association with Louis Armstrong.

segments.chapter: Meeting Louis and the New Orleans bands
segments.title: Returning from World War I and sitting in with Kid Ory at the 25
segments.summary: Punch returns in 1918-19 to find Louis Armstrong, Kid Ory and others at the 25; he sits in, plays army numbers and blues, and impresses the band.

segments.chapter: Meeting Louis and the New Orleans bands
segments.title: Playing Smiles, learned in the Army, in Ory's band
segments.summary: Punch learned Smiles in the Army and brought it into Ory's band; Louis did not know it then.

segments.chapter: Meeting Louis and the New Orleans bands
segments.title: Losing a trumpet and sleeping with the second one
segments.summary: Keys on his trumpet were ruined and the horn was lost; he paid for a replacement and jokes about keeping it in bed with him.

segments.chapter: Meeting Louis and the New Orleans bands
segments.title: Staying at Jack Carey's coal place
segments.summary: Punch lodged free in a coal shed owned by Jack Carey, whose band he joined; he slept on the daybed.

segments.chapter: Meeting Louis and the New Orleans bands
segments.title: Joining Jack Carey's band and starting his own band as Punch
segments.summary: Punch briefly played with another band, then joined Carey; people mistook him for Carey, so the men quit and formed a band under his own name.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and Louis in New Orleans
segments.title: Zulu parades and brass band players
segments.summary: Punch played Zulu parades for seven or eight years; he and the interviewers sort out the brass band lineup including a snare drummer, trombonist Frank Dusen and tuba player Willie Cornish.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and Louis in New Orleans
segments.title: Louis in the brass band, Black Benny and waving across the street
segments.summary: Punch says Black Benny looked after Louis, and that Louis passed his place nightly on the way to the 25, waving, before they joined at the next parade.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and Louis in New Orleans
segments.title: Recent contact with Louis and talk about his illness
segments.summary: Punch says he saw Louis at last year's festival and gets mail from him; the interviewers will contact Lucille and mention both men are sick.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and Louis in New Orleans
segments.title: Nicknames Punch, Bud and the twin Judah
segments.summary: Punch's only nickname outside the family is Punch; family called him Bud, and as a twin he and his brother were called Punch and Judah.

segments.title: Playing in the same brass band as Louis; meeting in Chicago
segments.summary: Punch and Louis played in the same brass band; they met in Chicago after Punch left New Orleans in 1927, and Louis put him with a band on Sundays.

segments.title: Cutting contest story with Joe and Russell Smith
segments.summary: At a club, Joe Smith packed up his horn after Punch's solo; they discuss Joe and Russell Smith's playing styles.

segments.title: Best audience: the Chicago-to-Memphis excursion and the vanishing promoter
segments.summary: Punch tells of earning five hundred dollars on percentage playing a Memphis excursion dance around 1928, and of a promoter who skipped out on pay.

segments.title: Young musicians, rock and roll and Preservation Hall audiences
segments.summary: Punch discusses why young people like Dixieland, mentions Japan and London, rock and roll, and young clarinetist Tommy Sancton.

segments.chapter: Army band and the Waifs' Home
segments.title: Army band at camp: size, parades and bugle duty
segments.summary: Punch describes the roughly 65-piece Army band where he learned music, and its daily parades.

segments.chapter: Army band and the Waifs' Home
segments.title: How he got into the Army brass band by playing bugle
segments.summary: Punch walked out of line to play a bugle call, was placed in the brass band and studied there; he knew only blues when he went in.

segments.title: Animal dance songs and singing Everybody's Doing It
segments.summary: Prompted about animal dances, Punch recalls older songs and sings Everybody's Doing It.

segments.title: Older than Louis; Satch's health; backyard musician Uncle August
segments.summary: Punch says he is four years older than Louis; talk turns to Satch's health, a friend's uncles, and Punch offers to sing Mama Loves Papa.

segments.title: Singing Mama Loves Papa and how he plays rock and roll
segments.summary: Punch sings Mama Loves Papa, says he seldom sings the old numbers and describes how a trumpet fits rock and roll.

segments.title: Knowing Louis from the Waifs' Home before the Army
segments.summary: Punch first met Louis in the Waifs' Home; Louis was just a bad boy who could not yet play, and Kid Rena was there.

segments.title: Kid Rena, Joe Rena and playing blues at fourteen
segments.summary: Punch wanted to stay in the home to learn music but was refused; at fourteen he played only blues for dances.

segments.title: Songs in the hospital and singing Cock Robin
segments.summary: Asked whether he misses singing in hospital, Punch sings Cock Robin; the interviewers recall an earlier visitor.

segments.title: Ring, luck and chatter
segments.summary: Interviewers chat with Punch about his good-luck ring, a visiting group, and the bulls song.

segments.title: Louis versus Lewis, Chicago job help and a message to Louis
segments.summary: Punch says they coined Satchmo, recalls Louis giving him jobs in Chicago before leaving for New York, and sends a get-well message.

segments.title: Playing the festival, and never dancing
segments.summary: Punch hopes to play the upcoming festival and says he never danced.

segments.title: Joining Petit, Morgan, Kelly and Ory after the Army
segments.summary: Punch came home from the Army and joined the leading bands; he learned Dogtown songs on the advertising wagon with Kid Ory.

segments.title: Idols; Louis, King Oliver and Mama Lucy
segments.summary: Punch says Louis' mother was King Oliver's sweetheart, which got Louis the second trumpet job; neither taught the other, and he asks after Louis' sister.

segments.title: Drinking at the saloon with Louis and Louis' smoking
segments.summary: Punch recalls the saloon where musicians drank, and the interviewers discuss Louis' drinking and smoking arrests, then agree to cut it.

segments.title: Starting to write songs in Chicago and losing them to copyists
segments.summary: Punch started writing songs in Chicago, writing notes down after working them out on his horn. Other players learned Punch's songs by ear and recorded them; he never copyrighted them and could do nothing.

segments.title: Singing That's My Home and others stealing his material
segments.summary: Punch sings That's My Home and says another musician stole many of his songs, though he recorded this one himself.

segments.title: Writing Back in the Old Days of New Orleans for an English visitor
segments.summary: Punch explains and sings his song Back in the Old Days of New Orleans, conceived after an English visitor asked about the city; he says he made it up.

segments.title: Dreaming songs and writing the words down
segments.summary: Punch describes dreaming songs, in picture form, and jumping up to write the words, the music coming easily.

segments.title: Singing songs he dreamed and worrying about copying
segments.summary: Punch sings lyrics from songs that came in dreams, shows the interviewers wiring, and tells them not to broadcast the song.

segments.title: No regrets, and learning bass drum and horn in the country
segments.summary: Punch says he never wanted to do anything but play music, and ran away from cutting cane. Working in the fields, Punch got the bass drum from the town brass band and taught himself horn; he says he taught Red Allen and Red's father taught him.

segments.title: Women players and trumpeter Dolly Hutchinson
segments.summary: Punch never taught women except trumpeter Dolly Hutchinson in Chicago, who learned from him daily and played tough.

segments.title: Where Red Allen got his ideas; Buddy Petit's harmonies
segments.summary: Punch says Red learned his fingering and freak notes around him; they discuss Buddy Petit's diminished chords and harmonic ideas.

segments.title: Louis' influences, King Oliver, and Kid Rena's range
segments.summary: Punch says Louis came up in King Oliver's style, got higher with his mouthpiece, and compares range with Kid Rena and Buddy Petit.

segments.title: Sam Morgan's band and the loving cup contest
segments.summary: Punch says Sam Morgan was not much on trumpet but had a good band, and tells of beating him for a loving cup with a waltz.

segments.title: Chris Kelly, Ike Morgan and Punch's years in Chicago
segments.summary: Punch rates Chris Kelly above Sam Morgan and discusses Sam's brother Ike, whom he found sick on his return from Chicago.

segments.title: Wanting to have heard Buddy Bolden; photographs
segments.summary: Punch regrets never seeing Buddy Bolden, whom people said drew dancers; the interviewers then talk about taking a good picture.

segments.title: Family news, hospital food and weight loss
segments.summary: Chat about his niece and great-nephew Lionel, ice water, lost weight and no-salt food.

segments.title: Lights in clubs, Preservation Hall travels and the dark 25
segments.summary: Asked about flashing lights, Punch says the darkest place he knew was the 25.
